title: Upper Mustang: trek or jeep
meta_description: Upper Mustang trek or jeep tour? Days, cost, altitude, comfort and what you see, compared, with the mixed itineraries we use most often.
summary: Trek if you have 12 to 15 days, enjoy walking six hours a day and want the old foot trails, villages and passes at walking pace. Take a jeep if you have 8 to 10 days, cannot walk long distances, or carry heavy camera gear. Many of our guests choose a mix: walk in, drive out.

sections.heading: Why this question exists at all
paras: Until the 2010s, there was only one way to reach Lo Manthang from Jomsom: on foot or on horseback, over four or five days of trail. Then a dirt road was pushed north up the Kali Gandaki, linking Jomsom with Lo Manthang and the Chinese border at Korala. Today jeeps, motorbikes and trucks use it every day in season.

The road changed life in Upper Mustang. Goods are cheaper, the sick can reach hospital, and villagers can sell apples and potatoes in Pokhara. It also changed the trek. Parts of the main trail now follow or cross the road, and in October you may share a stretch with a dusty line of jeeps. That is why the question of trek or jeep has become one of the first we discuss with anyone planning Upper Mustang.

sections.heading: The case for trekking
paras: Walking is still the best way to understand Upper Mustang. The trail between Chele and Ghami climbs over a series of passes where the view opens north into Lo one ridge at a time, and you feel the distance the old salt caravans covered. You arrive in villages tired and hungry, eat in lodge kitchens with families, and have time to wander after the walking is done. Most travellers who trek remember the evenings as much as the views.

Trekking also acclimatises you properly. Climbing from Kagbeni at 2,810 m to Lo Manthang at about 3,840 m over five days gives the body time to adjust. On foot you also reach places the jeeps do not: the trail by Ghar Gompa and Dhakmar, the high route through Samar, and quiet villages like Ghiling that sit away from the road.
list: You see the land at walking pace and arrive in villages the way local people did
Better acclimatisation and fewer altitude headaches
Trails to Ghar Gompa, Dhakmar and Samar that jeeps cannot follow
More time with lodge families and in monastery courtyards

sections.heading: The case for the jeep
paras: A jeep makes Lo Manthang possible for people who could never walk there. We have taken guests in their seventies, families with young children and travellers with knee problems to the walled city by road. With short driving days and stops in every village, it is a comfortable, if dusty, way to see a remarkable place.

The jeep also suits people short of time. A 9-night trip from Kathmandu fits into a two-week holiday with room for Kathmandu and Pokhara. And for photographers, a vehicle means heavy gear, tripods and the freedom to stop wherever the light is good. The trade-off is less time in villages, faster altitude gain and many hours on a rough road. Bring a buff, motion sickness tablets if needed, and patience. Ask your guide to plan short walks every day, to a monastery above the village or along an old section of trail, so you still spend part of each day on foot and meet people along the way.

sections.heading: Mixed itineraries we recommend
paras: In practice, many of our Upper Mustang trips are a mix. The commonest is to walk in and drive out: five or six days on foot from Kagbeni to Lo Manthang, two or three nights in the walled city, then a jeep back to Jomsom in one or two days. You get the acclimatisation and the best trails on the way up, and avoid walking back over the same ground.

Another option is to drive in as far as Ghami or Tsarang and then walk the most beautiful sections: Dhakmar and Ghar Gompa into Lo Manthang, or a loop to Chhoser on foot. A third is to drive both ways but add day walks, to Ghar Gompa, Chhoser or the hills above Lo Manthang, with the jeep waiting at the end. Each of these uses the restricted-area permit well, and each can be tailored to your fitness and time.

sections.heading: Altitude is the same either way
paras: A common mistake is to think a jeep trip carries no altitude risk. You sleep at the same height either way, about 3,840 m in Lo Manthang, and by jeep you get there faster. We always build in a night in Kagbeni at 2,810 m and a night at Tsarang or Ghami at around 3,500 m before Lo Manthang, and we carry a pulse oximeter. Drink three litres of water a day, avoid alcohol for the first nights up high, and tell your guide about headaches, nausea or breathlessness at rest.

Trekkers have the advantage of gradual ascent, but they also exert themselves more at altitude. Neither group is immune. If someone develops symptoms that do not ease with rest, the answer is to go down, and in Upper Mustang a jeep can usually get you down faster than walking.

sections.heading: Five questions to help you decide
paras: When guests cannot decide, we ask them a few simple questions. The answers usually make the choice obvious within a few minutes, and they also tell us which mixed itinerary might suit best. Be honest with yourself about fitness and time; Upper Mustang rewards people who travel at the pace that suits them, and punishes those who squeeze too much into too few days.

If most of your answers point the same way, follow them. If they are split, a walk-in, drive-out trip is almost always the right answer, because it gives you the best trail sections and the acclimatisation of walking without the long return over the same ground.
list: How many days do you have in Nepal in total, including Kathmandu and a spare day for flights?
Have you walked five to seven hours a day, several days in a row, on hilly ground before?
Do you have knee, back or heart problems that make long descents or bumpy roads hard?
Is meeting people in villages more important to you than seeing every monastery?
Will you carry heavy camera equipment or need to travel with young children or older relatives?

sections.heading: Season, road and flight notes
paras: The best months for both trek and jeep are April, May, September and October. Upper Mustang lies in the rain shadow of the Annapurnas and Dhaulagiri, so it can be visited in June, July and August when the rest of Nepal is wet, but the road below Jomsom and the Jomsom flights are more often disrupted then. From December to February many Lo Manthang families move south for the winter and lodges close.

Whichever way you go, the Jomsom flight is the weak link. It flies only in the morning, and wind or cloud cancels it often. Keep a spare day at the end of your trip, and if the flight does not go, the jeep road from Jomsom to Pokhara, 8 to 10 hours, is the fallback.

faqs.q: Is it better to trek or drive to Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: If you are fit and have 12 to 15 days, trekking gives a better experience: gradual acclimatisation, quieter trails and more time in villages. If you have less time or cannot walk long days, the jeep is a good option and still gets you three nights in Lo Manthang. Many people choose to walk in and drive out, which combines the advantages of both.

faqs.q: How long does the drive from Jomsom to Lo Manthang take?
faqs.a: About 6 to 8 hours of driving in a private 4WD jeep in dry conditions, longer after rain or landslides. We split it over two days with a night in Kagbeni and a night in Tsarang or Ghami, which helps acclimatisation and leaves time for stops at monasteries, caves and viewpoints.

faqs.q: Is the Upper Mustang trek still worth doing now there is a road?
faqs.a: Yes. The road follows the valley, but many sections of trail run separately, especially the high route via Samar, the route by Dhakmar and Ghar Gompa, and the paths around Chhoser. A good guide keeps you off the road most of the time. The villages, monasteries and landscapes are unchanged, and walking remains the best way to see them.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper, trek or jeep?
faqs.a: The jeep trip is usually cheaper in total because it is shorter, but the cost per day is higher because a private jeep is expensive. A 9-night jeep tour starts around USD 2,700 to 3,500 per person; a 14-night trek around USD 3,700 to 4,700, both including the USD 500 permit. Larger groups lower the jeep cost per person.

faqs.q: Can I hire a horse instead of walking?
faqs.a: Yes. Horses and ponies are a traditional way to travel in Upper Mustang, and you can hire one with a handler for some days or the whole trek. It is a good option for people who can walk a little but not six hours a day. Riding over passes is tiring in its own way, so build in rest.

faqs.q: Do jeep travellers need a guide in Upper Mustang?
faqs.a: Yes. The restricted-area permit requires a licensed guide whether you trek or drive, and a group of at least two foreigners. The driver does not count as your guide. Your guide also arranges lodges, explains monasteries and translates. Check current status before you travel, as rules change from time to time.

faqs.q: Is the road to Lo Manthang dangerous?
faqs.a: It is a rough mountain road with steep drops and river crossings, but it is driven daily in season by experienced local drivers. Risk is highest after heavy rain or in the monsoon, when landslides occur. We use well-maintained 4WD vehicles, avoid driving in bad weather, and change plans if the road is unsafe.

faqs.q: Can I combine the jeep tour with Muktinath?
faqs.a: Yes, and we recommend it. Muktinath is a short drive from Kagbeni and outside the restricted area, so it can be visited before or after Upper Mustang. Visiting first adds acclimatisation at about 3,700 m. Visiting after makes a good end to the trip, with dawn at the temple before you fly out of Jomsom.

faqs.q: Which option is best for photographers?
faqs.a: For most photographers the jeep, or a mix, works best. You can carry more gear, reach viewpoints at dawn and dusk, and stop when the light is right. Trekking photographers see more intimate scenes but carry less and often reach villages in harsh midday light. Our photography itinerary uses a jeep with short walks.
